citations.quote:
Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

**Constants are not unique and are not part of the data.** If $f$ is Lipschitz
with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with every constant $L' \ge L$, and likewise
for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). Let $a_0\in U$, let $h>0$ and $R>0$ satisfy $\overline B(a_0,R)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), put

$$M:=\sup_{x\in\overline B(a_0,R)}\|F(x)\|_2,\qquad L:=\text{a state-Lipschitz constant of }F\text{ on }\overline B(a_0,R),$$

so that $\|F(x)-F(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $x,y\in\overline B(a_0,R)$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and let $0\le\rho<R$ satisfy

$$hM\le R-\rho,\qquad Lh<1 .$$

Then for every $a\in\overline B(a_0,\rho)$ the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F(x(t)),\qquad x(0)=a$$

has exactly one solution $x(\,\cdot\,;a)$ on $[-h,h]$ whose graph lies in $[-h,h]\times\overline B(a_0,R)$, and for all $a,b\in\overline B(a_0,\rho)$ and all $s,t\in[-h,h]$:

1. $\|x(t;a)-x(t;b)\|_2\le e^{L|t|}\|a-b\|_2$;
2. $\|x(t;a)-x(s;a)\|_2\le M\,|t-s|$;
3. $\|x(t;a)-x(s;b)\|_2\le e^{Lh}\|a-b\|_2+M\,|t-s|$; in particular the map $(t,a)\mapsto x(t;a)$ is Lipschitz, hence continuous, on the compact set $[-h,h]\times\overline B(a_0,\rho)$.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ and $y:J\to\mathbb R^n$ solve the same IVP. The solution $y$ is an **extension** of $x$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $y|_I=x$. It is a proper extension when $I\subsetneq J$.

A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension. Its domain is its **maximal interval of existence**. A solution is **global** when its domain is the entire time projection allowed by the ODE domain; for a vector field on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, this means domain $\mathbb R$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Let $t_0<b$ be reals, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, and let $x:[t_0,b)\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0$$

on $[t_0,b)$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). Suppose there is a compact set $K\subseteq D$ and a real $\delta>0$ such that

$$\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b).$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a solution $\tilde x:[t_0,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ of the same initial value problem with $\tilde x(t)=x(t)$ for all $t\in[t_0,b)$; in particular $\tilde x(b)=\lim_{t\uparrow b}x(t)$ exists and lies in the state projection of $K$;
2. if moreover $D=\mathbb R\times U$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ is autonomous, $F(t,z)=G(z)$ with $G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and if there is a compact $K_0\subseteq U$ with $x(t)\in K_0$ for every $t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b)$, then the extension conclusion of clause 1 holds as well.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $n\ge1$, equip $\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), let $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and $z_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The Euclidean norm is a norm by [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], and the standard coordinate vectors form an ordered basis by [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]. For $A=(a_{ij})$ and $z\in\mathbb R^n$, define $(Az)_i:=\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}z_j$; this is a linear map by [[def-linear-map]], hence bounded by [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]], and $\|A\|$ denotes its induced Euclidean operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Matrix powers and products use [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]; their action agrees with composition of the corresponding linear maps by distributing the finite sums in the displayed coordinate formula. Define the **matrix exponential**

$$E:\mathbb R\longrightarrow M_n(\mathbb R),\qquad E(t):=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{t^k}{k!}A^k .$$

Then:

1. $E$ is well defined and of class $C^1$, with $E(0)=I_n$, $E(u+v)=E(u)E(v)$, $\frac{d}{du}E(u)=AE(u)=E(u)A$ for all $u,v\in\mathbb R$, and $\|E(u)\|\le e^{\|A\||u|}$ for the operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]) subordinate to the Euclidean norm.
2. The map
$$z:\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad z(t):=E(t-t_0)z_0+\int_{t_0}^tE(t-s)b(s)\,ds,$$
satisfies $z(t_0)=z_0$ and $z'(t)=A\,z(t)+b(t)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$.
3. Uniqueness: if $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with nonempty interior containing $t_0$ ([[def-interval]]) and $w:J\to\mathbb R^n$ is differentiable with $w'=Aw+b$ on $J$ and $w(t_0)=z_0$, then $w=z|_J$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

derivations.claim: Let $z$ be the maximal solution through $z_0$ and let $J\subseteq[0,\infty)$ be that part of its interval on which $\|z(t)\|_2\le r$; while $t\in J$, [F4] and the bound $\|F(z(s))\|_2\le L\|z(s)\|_2$ give $$\|z(t)\|_2\le\delta+\int_0^tL\|z(s)\|_2\,ds,$$ so [F5] yields $\|z(t)\|_2\le\delta e^{Lt}$ for all $t\in J$. In particular, if $t\in J$ and $t\le T$ then $\|z(t)\|_2\le\delta e^{LT}<r$.

The maximal solution is defined on all of $[0,T]$. Indeed, if its forward interval ended at some $\tau\le T$, then the graph of $z$ on $[0,\tau)$ would lie in the compact set $[0,T]\times\overline B(0,r)$ by step 1.1 applied on $J\cap[0,\tau)$ — more precisely, should $z$ reach $\|z\|_2=r$ at some first time $\tau_0$, step 1.1 would give $\|z(\tau_0)\|_2\le\delta e^{L\tau_0}\le\delta e^{LT}<r$ at that time, a contradiction; so $\|z(t)\|_2<r$ for all $t$ in the maximal forward interval that are $\le T$, and the graph stays in the compact subset $[0,T]\times\overline B(0,r)\subseteq[0,T]\times U$. By [F3] the solution extends past every finite endpoint below or at $T$, so it is defined on $[0,T]$ and step 1.1 gives $\|z(t)\|_2\le\delta e^{Lt}$ there; this is clause 1.

Finite-interval comparison identity: on $[0,T]$ put $q:=z-y$ and $b(t):=F(z(t))-Az(t)$. The curve $b$ is continuous on $[0,T]$, and $q'=Aq+b$, $q(0)=0$. Define $r(t):=E(-t)q(t)$. By [F6], the chain rule and product rule, $$r'(t)=-AE(-t)q(t)+E(-t)(Aq(t)+b(t))=E(-t)b(t),$$ since $AE(-t)=E(-t)A$. The vector-valued fundamental theorem of calculus, applied on the actual interval $[0,T]$, gives $r(t)=\int_0^tE(-s)b(s)\,ds$; multiplying by $E(t)$ and using [F6]'s group law yields $$q(t)=\int_0^tE(t-s)b(s)\,ds.$$ This derivation uses only the continuous values of $b$ on $[0,T]$. Consequently, using $\|E(t-s)\|\le e^{\|A\|(t-s)}$ for $0\le s\le t$, the quadratic remainder hypothesis and clause 1, $$\|z(t)-y(t)\|_2\le\int_0^t e^{\|A\|(t-s)}\bigl\|F(z(s))-Az(s)\bigr\|_2\,ds\le C\delta^2\int_0^te^{\|A\|(t-s)}e^{2Ls}\,ds,$$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

For the final estimate, $e^{\|A\|(t-s)}\le e^{\|A\|t}$ and $e^{2Ls}\le e^{2Lt}$ on $0\le s\le t$, so $\int_0^te^{\|A\|(t-s)}e^{2Ls}ds\le t\,e^{(\|A\|+2L)t}$; substituting into step 3.1 gives the displayed product bound. This proves clause 2.

boundaries.reason: No empty set occurs: U is open and contains the closed ball of radius r, so the ball is nonempty.
The datum is required to satisfy delta>0; the equilibrium datum is excluded by hypothesis, and no claim is made for it.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 tracks a single trajectory from z0 through the trapping argument; no family of data is quantified in the proof.
Step 2.1 treats the marginal case where the trajectory would reach the boundary |z|=r, showing the smallness condition delta e^{LT}<r prevents it.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 cover [0,T] including t=0 and t=T, and the time integration in step 3.1 is over [0,t] with t<=T.

boundaries.reason: No choice principle is used: the cylinder constants and the extension argument are explicit.
The statement is a conditional estimate, not an equivalence.
The statement is a conditional estimate, not an equivalence.

risk_review.notes: Remainder bound implies F(0)=0. delta>0 and strict delta exp(LT)<r give a first-exit contradiction and compact continuation through T. Although J in step 1.1 is loosely described, step 2.1 applies the estimate on the connected initial pre-exit interval explicitly. Integrating factor E(-t)(z-y) uses only forcing on [0,T]; norm bounds give the two estimates. C=0,L=0 and t=0 are valid.

citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $n\ge1$, $P>0$, $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open, and let $f:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, continuously partially differentiable in the second variable and $P$-periodic in time, with average $\bar f$, oscillatory part $f-\bar f$ and periodic deviation $g$ as in [[def-cm-averaging-data-and-averaged-field]] ([[def-interval]]). Here $D_xf(t,x):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ denotes the total derivative in the state variable, with coordinate columns $\partial_{x_j}f(t,x)$; it exists and is continuous by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]. The same notation is used for $D_x\bar f$ and $D_xg$ when those total derivatives exist. Let $x_0\in O$, $R>0$ with $\overline B(x_0,R)\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) and let $M,L\ge0$ satisfy

$$\|f(t,x)\|_2\le M,\qquad \|f(t,x)-f(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(t\in\mathbb R,\ x,y\in\overline B(x_0,R)).$$

Then:

1. $\|\bar f(x)\|_2\le M$ and $\|\bar f(x)-\bar f(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $x,y\in\overline B(x_0,R)$.
2. $g$ is $P$-periodic and $\|g(t,x)\|_2\le2MP$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$ and $x\in\overline B(x_0,R)$; moreover $\|g(t,x)-g(t,y)\|_2\le2LP\|x-y\|_2$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$ and $x,y\in\overline B(x_0,R)$.
3. $\partial_tg(t,x)=f(t,x)-\bar f(x)$ for every $(t,x)$; consequently $\|\partial_tg(t,x)\|_2\le2M$ for $x\in\overline B(x_0,R)$ and $\|\partial_tg(t,x)-\partial_tg(t,y)\|_2\le2L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$ and $x,y\in\overline B(x_0,R)$.
4. $g$ has continuous first partial derivatives on $\mathbb R\times O$; its partial derivative in the second variable is $D_xg(t,x)=\int_0^t\bigl(D_xf(s,x)-D_x\bar f(x)\bigr)ds$, and $\|D_xg(t,x)\|\le2LP$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, $x\in\overline B(x_0,R)$, with $\|\cdot\|$ the operator norm on $M_n(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). In particular $g$ is totally differentiable at every point of $\mathbb R\times O$ ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]).

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $F$ is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time**, if every compact time-state cylinder $C\subseteq D$ has a finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x),(t,y)\in C$ have the same time coordinate.

On every compact time-state cylinder the state-variable inequality holds with one finite constant $L$. More generally, let $p\ge1$, let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, let $D_\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\Lambda$ be open in its relative Euclidean topology, and let $F:D_\Lambda\to\mathbb R^n$. The parameter family is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters** when every compact time-state-parameter cylinder $C\subseteq D_\Lambda$ has one finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x,\lambda)-F(t,y,\lambda)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x,\lambda),(t,y,\lambda)\in C$ have the same time and parameter coordinates.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ and $y:J\to\mathbb R^n$ solve the same IVP. The solution $y$ is an **extension** of $x$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $y|_I=x$. It is a proper extension when $I\subsetneq J$.

A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension. Its domain is its **maximal interval of existence**. A solution is **global** when its domain is the entire time projection allowed by the ODE domain; for a vector field on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, this means domain $\mathbb R$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Let $t_0<b$ be reals, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, and let $x:[t_0,b)\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0$$

on $[t_0,b)$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). Suppose there is a compact set $K\subseteq D$ and a real $\delta>0$ such that

$$\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b).$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a solution $\tilde x:[t_0,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ of the same initial value problem with $\tilde x(t)=x(t)$ for all $t\in[t_0,b)$; in particular $\tilde x(b)=\lim_{t\uparrow b}x(t)$ exists and lies in the state projection of $K$;
2. if moreover $D=\mathbb R\times U$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ is autonomous, $F(t,z)=G(z)$ with $G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and if there is a compact $K_0\subseteq U$ with $x(t)\in K_0$ for every $t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b)$, then the extension conclusion of clause 1 holds as well.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

derivations.claim: By [F2] let $x:(\alpha,\beta)\to O$ be the unique maximal solution of $x'=\varepsilon f(t,x)$ with $x(0)=x_0$, where $\alpha<0<\beta$. Define $\tau_R:=\inf\{t\in[0,\beta):\|x(t)-x_0\|_2=R\}$, with $\tau_R:=+\infty$ if this set is empty, and $T_0:=\min\{A/\varepsilon,\beta,\tau_R\}$. For $0\le t<T_0$ one has $x(t)\in B(x_0,R)$, so the bounds of [F1] apply; also $g$ is totally differentiable near $(t,x(t))$, as required by [F3].

Estimate on $[0,T_0)$. Put $d(t):=x(t)-\varepsilon g(t,x(t))$ and $w:=d-y$. Since $g(0,x_0)=0$, $w(0)=0$. By [F3] and $\partial_tg=f-\bar f$, $$d'=\varepsilon f-\varepsilon\bigl(\partial_tg+D_xg\cdot x'\bigr)=\varepsilon f-\varepsilon(f-\bar f)-\varepsilon^2D_xg\cdot f=\varepsilon\bar f(x)-\varepsilon^2D_xg(t,x)f(t,x),$$ so $w'=\varepsilon\bigl(\bar f(x)-\bar f(y)\bigr)-\varepsilon^2D_xg(t,x)f(t,x)$ for $0\le t<T_0$. Using [F1], $\|\bar f(x)-\bar f(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2\le L\|w\|_2+\varepsilon LB$ because $\|x-y\|_2\le\|x-d\|_2+\|d-y\|_2=\varepsilon\|g(t,x(t))\|_2+\|w\|_2\le\varepsilon B+\|w\|_2$, and $\|\varepsilon^2D_xg\cdot f\|_2\le\varepsilon^2B_1M$. Therefore, by [F4], $$\|w(t)\|_2\le\int_0^t\bigl(\varepsilon L\|w(s)\|_2+\varepsilon^2(LB+B_1M)\bigr)ds,$$ and the Gronwall inequality of [F4] with $L_0=0$, $M_0=\varepsilon^2(LB+B_1M)$, $K_0=\varepsilon L$ gives $\|w(t)\|_2\le\varepsilon^2(LB+B_1M)\,t\,e^{\varepsilon Lt}\le\varepsilon(LB+B_1M)A\,e^{LA}$ for $t<T_0\le A/\varepsilon$. Hence $$\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2\le\|w(t)\|_2+\varepsilon B\le\varepsilon\bigl[B+(LB+B_1M)Ae^{LA}\bigr]\le\varepsilon K.$$

No exit and continuation. If $\tau_R<\min\{\beta,A/\varepsilon\}$, continuity lets the estimate of step 2.1 pass to $t=\tau_R$; then $$R=\|x(\tau_R)-x_0\|_2\le\|x(\tau_R)-y(\tau_R)\|_2+\|y(\tau_R)-x_0\|_2\le\varepsilon K+(R-\rho)<R,$$ a contradiction. Hence for every $0\le t<\min\{\beta,A/\varepsilon\}$, step 2.1 and the hypothesis on $y$ give $\|x(t)-x_0\|_2\le\varepsilon K+(R-\rho)<R$. If $\beta\le A/\varepsilon$ were finite, the graph of $x$ near $\beta$ would stay in the compact subset $[0,A/\varepsilon]\times\overline B(x_0,R)$ of $[0,\infty)\times O$, so compact continuation [F2] would extend $x$ past $\beta$, contradicting maximality. Thus $\beta>A/\varepsilon$, and $x$ is defined on all of $[0,A/\varepsilon]$; continuity extends the estimate of step 2.1 to the endpoint, proving the claim.

boundaries.reason: No empty set occurs: O is open and contains the closed ball of radius R, and the horizon [0,A/epsilon] is nondegenerate.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 evaluates the conjugated difference at t=0 and step 3.1 compares at the first exit time; the datum x0 is a single point.
Step 3.1 derives the estimate on the single interval [0,T*] with the horizon A/epsilon and the trapping radius rho as the only scale parameters.
Step 3.1 uses the strict trapping margin epsilon K<rho and shows that the boundary |x-x0|=R cannot be reached; the boundary case epsilon K=rho is excluded by hypothesis.
Step 3.1 controls the endpoint T*=A/epsilon of the horizon and the maximal-interval endpoint by compact continuation.

Let $\varepsilon>0$, let $\widehat J,\widehat S\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open intervals, and let $J\subseteq\widehat J$ and $S\subseteq\widehat S$ be intervals with nonempty interiors ([[def-interval]]). Let $h:\widehat J\times\widehat S\to\mathbb R$ and $k:\widehat J\times\mathbb R\times\widehat S\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ on these open Euclidean domains ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and suppose $k$ is $2\pi$-periodic in its second variable on $J\times\mathbb R\times S$:

$$k(I,\theta+2\pi,s)=k(I,\theta,s)\qquad\text{for all }(I,\theta,s)\in J\times\mathbb R\times S .$$

The **transformed Hamiltonian** of the datum is

$$K(I,\theta,s):=h(I,s)+\varepsilon\,k(I,\theta,s),$$

its **frequency function** is

$$\omega(I,s):=\partial_Ih(I,s),$$

its **angle average** is $\langle k\rangle(I,s):=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}k(I,\theta,s)\,d\theta$, and, on the set where $\omega\ne0$, its **drift generator** is

$$g(I,\theta,s):=\frac{k(I,\theta,s)-\langle k\rangle(I,s)}{\omega(I,s)} .$$

The **branch vector field** of the datum is the restriction to $J\times\mathbb R\times S$ of the map $\widehat\Phi:\widehat J\times\mathbb R\times\widehat S\to\mathbb R^3$,

$$\widehat\Phi(I,\theta,s):=\Bigl(-\varepsilon\,\partial_\theta k(I,\theta,s),\ \ \partial_Ih(I,s)+\varepsilon\,\partial_Ik(I,\theta,s),\ \ \varepsilon\Bigr),$$

and a **branch solution** on an interval $T\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a differentiable $(I,\theta,s):T\to J\times\mathbb R\times S$ satisfying $(I,\theta,s)'=\widehat\Phi(I,\theta,s)$ at every $t\in T$, with derivatives relative to $T$ at included endpoints. On open time intervals this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $\widehat J\times\mathbb R\times\widehat S$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). Partial derivatives are those of the ambient Euclidean coordinates.

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

components and their limits are as in

> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k>0$, and consider the homogeneous damped oscillator model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero, with characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k$, discriminant $\Delta=c^2-4mk$, damping rate $\gamma:=c/(2m)$, and, when applicable, roots
$$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \lambda:=-\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^2}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0).$$

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Distinct real roots.** If $\Delta>0$, then $\lambda_+>\lambda_-$ are exactly the real roots of $p$, and a function $x:J\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a solution of the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

2. **Double real root.** If $\Delta=0$, then $\lambda=-c/(2m)$ is the only root of $p$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{\lambda t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

3. **Complex conjugate roots.** If $\Delta<0$, then $\omega>0$, the roots of $p$ are $-\gamma\pm i\omega$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

4. **Initial data.** In each of the three cases and for every $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$ there is exactly one solution $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $x'(0)=v_0$. Its coefficients are
$$A=\frac{v_0-\lambda_-x_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-},\quad B=\frac{\lambda_+x_0-v_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\quad(\Delta>0),\qquad A=x_0,\ B=v_0-\lambda x_0\quad(\Delta=0),$$
$$A=x_0,\quad B=\frac{v_0+\gamma x_0}{\omega}\quad(\Delta<0).$$

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, let $k\le0$, and consider the model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero. In the three cases below, $x:J\to\mathbb R$ runs over solutions on intervals $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior.

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Double zero root ($k=0$, $c=0$).** Then on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if $x(t)=A+Bt$ for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a unique global member of this family. For every datum $(x_0,v_0)$ there is a unique global solution on $\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$, namely $x(t)=x_0+v_0t$.
2. **Simple zero root ($k=0$, $c>0$).** Then on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if
$$x(t)=A+Be^{-ct/m}$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a unique global member of this family. For every datum $(x_0,v_0)$ there is a unique global solution on $\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$, namely the member with $A=x_0+\frac{m v_0}{c}$ and $B=-\frac{m v_0}{c}$. This global solution has limit $A$ as $t\to+\infty$; any local solution on an interval unbounded above has the same limit along that interval.
3. **One positive and one negative root ($k<0$).** Put $$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt{c^2-4mk}}{2m}.$$ Then $\lambda_-<0<\lambda_+$, both are real roots of the characteristic polynomial, and on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a global member of this family. In particular the global solution $t\mapsto e^{\lambda_+t}$ has data $x(0)=1$, $x'(0)=\lambda_+$ and satisfies $e^{\lambda_+t}\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$: the model has an unbounded solution growing exponentially on $[0,\infty)$.

Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, let $f_0\in\mathbb R$ and $\Omega\ge0$, and consider the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f$ with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(t)=f_0\cos(\Omega t)$ ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]). Put

is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$. Its amplitude about zero is $|f_0|/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$.

$$x_p(t):=\frac{f_0\,t\sin(\omega_0t)}{2m\omega_0}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$; if $f_0\ne0$ then $x_p$ is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$.

$$x(t)=x_p(t)+x_h(t)$$
where $x_h$ is a homogeneous solution; consequently $x(t)-x_p(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]) and $x$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$.

$$\|F(z)-Az\|_2\le C\|z\|_2^2,\qquad \|F(z)\|_2\le L\|z\|_2\qquad(\|z\|_2\le r),$$
where $Az$ and $\|A\|$ use the matrix-action and induced Euclidean operator-norm convention of [[cor-cm-variation-of-constants-for-linear-systems]].

Let $z_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\delta:=\|z_0\|_2>0$, let $T>0$ with $\delta e^{LT}<r$, and let $y:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be the solution of the linear system $y'=Ay$, $y(0)=z_0$ ([[cor-cm-variation-of-constants-for-linear-systems]]). Then:

1. The maximal solution $z$ of $z'=F(z)$, $z(0)=z_0$ is defined on $[0,T]$ and satisfies $\|z(t)\|_2\le\delta e^{Lt}$ for $t\in[0,T]$ ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]).
2. For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|z(t)-y(t)\|_2\le C\delta^2\int_0^te^{\|A\|(t-s)}e^{2Ls}\,ds\le C\delta^2\,t\,e^{(\|A\|+2L)t},$$
where $\|A\|$ is the operator norm of $A$ for the Euclidean norm ([[def-operator-norm]]).

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For all real $x,y$,

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Growth bound: if $\theta\ne0$, the mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]) applied to $\sin$ between $0$ and $\theta$, with $|\cos|\le1$ from [L4], gives $|\sin\theta|=|\sin\theta-\sin0|\le|\theta|$; this inequality is immediate at $\theta=0$. Thus $\|F(z)\|_2^2=\omega^2+\sin^2\theta\le\omega^2+\theta^2=\|z\|_2^2$, so $L=1$ is admissible. With $\delta=1/100$ and $T=1$, [L4] gives $\delta e^{LT}=e/100<3/100<1/20<1/2=r$, so the hypotheses of [L1] hold.

Substitute: by [L1] and [L3], for $0\le t\le1$ the error is at most $\tfrac1{12}\delta^2\int_0^t e^{(1-s)}e^{2s}ds\le\tfrac1{12}\delta^2\int_0^1 e^{(1-s)}e^{2s}ds$, since the integrand is positive by [L4]. The addition formula gives $e^{(1-s)}e^{2s}=e^{1+s}$; since $0\le s\le1$, monotonicity gives $e^{1+s}\le e^2<9$ by [L4]. Monotonicity of the integral [L5] therefore yields $\int_0^1e^{1+s}ds\le9$, and the error is at most $\tfrac1{12}\cdot10^{-4}\cdot9=\tfrac34\cdot10^{-4}<10^{-4}$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $P>0$, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]). Assume that for each standard coordinate vector $e_j$ of $\mathbb R^n$, $0\le j<n$, and every $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times O$, the vector-valued derivative at $r=0$ of $r\mapsto f(t,x+r e_j)$ exists, and that each resulting partial derivative $(t,x)\mapsto\partial_{x_j}f(t,x)$ is continuous on $\mathbb R\times O$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). This is the meaning of **continuously partially differentiable in the state variable** here. Suppose also that $f$ is **$P$-periodic in time**, that is

$$f(t+P,x)=f(t,x)\qquad\text{for all }(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times O .$$

The **average** of such an $f$ is the map

$$\bar f:O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad \bar f(x):=\frac1P\int_0^Pf(s,x)\,ds,$$

where the integral is the componentwise Riemann integral of the continuous curve $s\mapsto f(s,x)$ over the compact interval $[0,P]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]); it is well defined and finite for every $x\in O$ because that curve is continuous. The **oscillatory part** of $f$ is $f-\bar f$, and the **deviation** of $f$ is

$$g:[0,P]\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad g(t,x):=\int_0^t\bigl(f(s,x)-\bar f(x)\bigr)\,ds .$$

Because $\int_0^Pf(s,x)-\bar f(x)\,ds=P\bar f(x)-P\bar f(x)=0$ by linearity and additivity of the integral ([[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]), the formula $g(t+kP,x):=g(t,x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\in[0,P)$ defines a unique extension, again written $g$, to all of $\mathbb R\times O$; it satisfies $g(t+P,x)=g(t,x)$ and $g(0,x)=0$ for all $(t,x)$, and on $[0,P]$ it is the integral displayed above.

The **averaged (or reduced) system** of $f$ for a parameter $\varepsilon>0$ is the autonomous first-order system on $O$

$$y'(t)=\varepsilon\,\bar f(y(t)).$$

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],
   [[def-the-integral-function]]) and is a primitive of $f$ on $I$.
2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**The scope is exactly the continuous case, and that is not a limitation of the
proof.** An integrable function need not have a primitive, and a function with a
primitive need not be integrable; this corollary is precisely the intersection
where both fundamental theorems apply, and both witnesses are on the companion
page.

where $\varepsilon>0$ and $A>0$ are parameters. Suppose $y:[0,A/\varepsilon]\to\overline B(x_0,R-\rho)$ is a solution of the averaged system
